description_full: General Dynamics Corporation operates as an aerospace and defense company worldwide. It operates through four segments: Aerospace, Marine Systems, Combat Systems, and Technologies. The Aerospace segment produces and sells business jets; and offers aircraft maintenance and repair, management, aircraft-on-ground support, customer support and custom completion services, modifications, upgrades, and lifecycle sustainment support services. The Marine Systems segment designs and builds nuclear-powered submarines, surface combatants, and auxiliary ships for the United States Navy and Jones Act ships for commercial customers, as well as provides maintenance, modernization, and lifecycle support services for navy ships; offers and program management, planning, engineering, and design support services for submarine construction programs. The Combat Systems segment manufactures land combat solutions, such as wheeled and tracked combat vehicles, Stryker wheeled combat vehicles, piranha vehicles, weapons systems, energetics and munitions, mobile bridge systems with payloads, tactical vehicles, main battle tanks, and armored vehicles; and offers modernization programs, support and sustainment services, and development programs. The Technologies segment provides information technology solutions and mission support services; mobile communication, computers, and command-and-control mission systems; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance solutions to military, intelligence, and federal civilian customers; cloud services, cybersecurity, network modernization, artificial intelligence; machine learning; application development, high-performance computing, and 5G and advanced communications services; and unmanned undersea vehicle manufacturing and assembly services. The company was founded in 1899 and is headquartered in Reston, Virginia.

financial_summary: General Dynamics Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $95.7B market cap on $52.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $4.0B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.22× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.6×.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $8.2M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Significant goodwill (37% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 8% over 3 months
Industrials ETF trading well below its long-term trend
Cyclical sectors like Industrials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
47 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.93x).
It accounts for 1.4% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.63, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $408.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 15% in the 2022 bear market and 61% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 2% below its DCF fair value of $362, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $276 to $487 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 58% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $417 on average, 18% above the price.
The price implies 7.8% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 7.8%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.22x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($2.3B of cash against $8.0B of debt), with interest covered 10.6x.
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.1% over 3 years, 6.7% over 5 years and 5.3% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 26% of profits supports about 3.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.52 (orders outpacing sales) and a backlog worth 2.2x annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 2.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and institutions hold 87%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $8.2M sold).
It returns 2.3% a year to shareholders (0.7% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 47 consecutive years, raising it 5.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 117,000 employees, each generates about $449K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 3.2% a year.
That works out to $34K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.2M (18x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
